p.src: Tong Guan took command of the central army as supreme commander. Once the orders had been issued and all ranks of the three armies were ready, weapons were released from the imperial arsenal, and an auspicious day was chosen for the expedition. Grand Marshals Gao and Yang arranged a farewell banquet, while the court ordered the Secretariat to reward the troops. Tong Guan had already assembled his generals. The next day he sent the vanguard out of the city, then took leave of the emperor, sprang upon his horse, and rode through the New Cao Gate. At the roadside pavilion five li beyond the city, he found Grand Marshals Gao and Yang waiting with the assembled officials. Tong Guan dismounted. Grand Marshal Gao raised a cup and said to him, “Your Excellency the Commissioner will surely render great service to the court on this expedition. May you soon return with songs of victory. These bandits lurk among the marshes. You need only cut off their provisions on every side, fortify your stockades, and lure them down from the mountain before advancing. Then every one of them may be taken alive, and you will prove worthy of the trust the court has placed in you.” Tong Guan replied, “I am deeply grateful for your counsel and shall not forget it.” When they had drunk, Grand Marshal Yang also raised a cup and said to Tong Guan, “Your Excellency has long studied the military classics and thoroughly understands the arts of war. To destroy and capture these bandits will be as easy as turning your hand. The one difficulty is that they lurk among the lakes and marshes, where the terrain is unfavorable to us. But when Your Excellency arrives there, you will surely devise an excellent plan.” Tong Guan said, “Once I arrive, I shall act as circumstances require. I have my methods.” Grand Marshals Gao and Yang offered him wine together and congratulated him, saying, “Beyond the capital gate, we shall eagerly await your victorious return.” After taking leave, they each mounted their horses. Officials from every government office came to see him on his way, too many to count. Some accompanied him a short way and others a long way, then returned to the capital one after another; there is no need to recount it all. p.src: The soldiers formed nine divisions, their banners arrayed in the colors of the five directions. Dark-green spears, tempered-steel spears, and raven-horn spears spread their gleam across the fields; Green Dragon sabers, crescent-moon sabers, and goose-feather sabers filled the heavens with a murderous air. Sparrow-painted bows, iron-cored bows, and richly carved bows were thrust in pairs into flying-fish cases; tiger-shooting arrows, wolf-fang arrows, and willow-leaf arrows clustered together in lion quivers. Birchwood crossbows, lacquered crossbows, and foot-drawn crossbows filled the ranks of the vanguard; mountain-cleaving axes, crescent axes, and flowered battle-axes followed close behind the central divisions. Bamboo-jointed whips, tiger-eye whips, and polished-steel whips all hung at the warriors’ elbows; meteor hammers, heart-shaped hammers, and flying-claw hammers were carried at their sides. From the sky-rending halberds, leopard tails fluttered; the eighteen-foot spears were wound with strings of pearls. Dragon-patterned swords flashed like broad pools of autumn water, while tiger-headed shields bore painted wisps of spring cloud. The fierce and valiant vanguard led elite troops who could uproot mountains and clear the way; the heroic marshal commanded stalwarts who could shout rivers dry and sever bridges. Commanders of the left and right displayed magnificent courage and strategy; distant scouts and near scouts galloped with awe-inspiring might. Drums that shook the heavens made the mountains tremble; sunlit banners put ghosts and spirits to flight.

p.src: That day Tong Guan left the Eastern Capital and advanced steadily onward. Within a day or two, he had reached the borders of Jizhou. Prefect Zhang Shuye came out of the city to welcome him, while the great army encamped outside the walls. Tong Guan led a light cavalry detachment into the city and dismounted before the prefectural offices. Zhang Shuye invited him into the main hall. When their formal greetings were over, Zhang stood respectfully before him. Commissioner Tong said, “The bandits of the marshes murder innocent people, plunder merchants and travelers, and commit wickedness of every kind. Past campaigns against them repeatedly failed because the right men were not appointed, allowing the evil to spread. Now I command a great army of one hundred thousand and a hundred battle generals. On the appointed day I shall sweep the stronghold clean, seize every bandit, and bring peace to the people.” Zhang Shuye replied, “Your Excellency, these bandits lurk among the lakes and marshes. Though they are lawless outlaws of the hills and forests, many among them are resourceful, brave, and formidable men. Do not let anger drive you to lead the army headlong against them. Only through sound strategy can success be won.” Tong Guan flew into a rage on hearing this and cursed him: “Cowardly wretches like you fear blades and flee from swords, clinging to life and dreading death. You have ruined affairs of state and allowed the bandits to grow so powerful. Now that I have come, what is there to fear?” Zhang Shuye dared say no more and merely prepared food and wine for his guest. Commissioner Tong immediately left the city. The next day he drove the great army onward and made camp near Liangshan Marsh.

p.src: The mounted general approaching them was plainly identified by the inscription on his standard: “Chief Patrol Commander Zhang Qing, the Featherless Arrow.” Gong Wang rode on his left and Ding Desun on his right. They scouted straight up to Tong Guan’s army, reined in scarcely a hundred paces away, and turned back. The two vanguard generals of the front division had received no orders and dared not move rashly. Word was sent to the center, and Commander-in-Chief Tong Guan came personally to the front. Before he had finished observing, Zhang Qing rode out scouting once more. Tong Guan was about to send men in pursuit and challenge him, but those beside him said, “The brocade pouch behind his saddle is full of stones, and he never misses when he casts one. He must not be pursued.” Zhang Qing made three scouting passes in succession. Seeing that Tong Guan still would not advance, he withdrew. He had gone less than five li when gongs sounded behind the mountain, and five hundred infantrymen wheeled into view. At their head came four infantry chiefs—Li Kui the Black Whirlwind, Fan Rui the Demon King of Chaos, Xiang Chong the Eight-Armed Nezha, and Li Gun the Great Sage Who Soars to Heaven—charging straight forward. Before and behind are arrayed the forms of Tortoise and Serpent; left and right are divided into the shapes of Dragon and Tiger. On the left, azure vapors coil below; on the right, white radiance streams through the ranks. Golden clouds fill the center, while the Yellow Way conforms entirely to wu and ji. At the four corners stand the divisions of the Twenty-Eight Mansions, and around the whole circuit unfold the transformations of the Sixty-Four Hexagrams. Winding and twisting, amid seeming disorder the ranks change into a long serpent; ordered and exact, in stillness their majesty resembles a crouching tiger. p.src: From the command platform within his formation, Privy Councilor Tong Guan fixed his eyes upon the troops of Liangshan Marsh. In scarcely any time they had deployed into this Nine Palaces and Eight Trigrams formation. Its soldiers and horsemen were valiant, its officers and warriors heroic; the sight so terrified him that his soul fled and his courage failed. Over and over he exclaimed, “Now I understand why every government army sent here to suppress them has returned in crushing defeat. So this is how formidable they are!” After watching for some time, he heard the gongs and drums challenging them to battle sound without cease in Song Jiang’s army. Tong Guan descended from the command platform, mounted his warhorse, and rode again to the generals in the vanguard. “Who dares go out to fight and challenge them?” he asked. A fierce general emerged from the vanguard ranks, boldly spurred his horse forward, then leaned from the saddle and reported to Tong Guan, “I am willing to go. I beg Your Excellency’s command.” It was Chen Zhu, military commissioner of Zhengzhou, now serving as deputy vanguard commander. He wore a white robe and silver armor, rode a dark horse with a crimson tassel, and wielded a great long-shafted saber. Tong Guan ordered the gongs and drums beneath the standard to sound three rolls, while from the command platform a red flag was waved to marshal the troops. Chen Zhu galloped out beneath the gate standard, and both armies raised a thunderous shout together. Chen Zhu reined in his horse, leveled his saber, and shouted fiercely, “Groundless bandits! Treasonous madmen! Heaven’s army has arrived, yet still you will not surrender. Must you wait until flesh and bones are pounded into mire? Then repentance will come too late!” From Song Jiang’s formation due south, the vanguard chieftain and Tiger General Qin Ming galloped forth. Without exchanging a word, he swung up his wolf-toothed mace and charged straight at Chen Zhu. The two horses met and both weapons rose: the mace wielder struck straight at his opponent’s head, while the saber wielder hacked directly at his face. The two generals wheeled back and forth, clashing again and again for more than twenty bouts. Qin Ming deliberately showed an opening and let Chen Zhu pursue him in; Chen Zhu’s saber then cut only empty air. Seizing the moment, Qin Ming raised his mace and brought it down. It smashed squarely through Chen Zhu’s helmet and crown into the top of his skull, and Chen Zhu toppled dead beneath his horse. Qin Ming’s two lieutenants, Shan Tinggui and Wei Dingguo, galloped straight out of the formation, seized the fine horse first, and then withdrew in support of Qin Ming. Beneath the gate standard in the southeast, the Tiger General Dong Ping, known as the “Double-Speared General,” saw Qin Ming win the first distinction and thought in the saddle, “Our great army has already surged forward in fighting spirit. If I do not charge through now and capture Tong Guan, what better moment could there be?” He gave a great shout like a thunderclap bursting before the lines, gripped a spear in each hand, slapped his horse, and charged straight into the enemy formation. Seeing this, Tong Guan wheeled his horse around and fled toward the central army. Beneath the gate standard in the southwest, the swift cavalry general Suo Chao, known as the “Impatient Vanguard,” also cried, “If we do not capture Tong Guan here and now, what better moment could there be?” Swinging his great ax, he cut his way into the formation. When Qin Ming in the center saw the two wings charging through, he too waved his own unit’s red standard into motion, and all his troops surged into the enemy ranks together to capture Tong Guan. It was truly like several black eagles pursuing a purple swallow, or a pack of fierce tigers devouring a lamb. As for whether Privy Councilor Tong Guan escaped with his life, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
